name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,802

entries.clue: No good getting into silly sodding rows (4-5)

indicatorNotes.silly: SODDING is rearranged, made nonsense of

blocks.note: NG is the standard abbreviation for no good

annotation.surface: Someone fed up with pointless, foul-mouthed quarrels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Silly' looks like part of the swearing but is the anagram signal; 'sodding' is British mild profanity. A ding-dong is a British term for a noisy row.
annotation.definitionFit: A ding-dong is informal British English for a heated argument, so ding-dongs are rows.

entries.clue: Returning soldiers spoken about abusively? Jesus! (9)

indicatorNotes.Returning: turns the whole string back to front, read from the end

blocks.note: to revile is to speak of someone abusively

annotation.surface: Someone exclaims in shock at hearing troops being badmouthed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jesus!' reads as an oath, but it is the definition: the Deliverer is a title for Christ. 'Returning' sits first but governs the whole wordplay, soldiers and all, so the reversal also reorders the two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Christ is called the Deliverer, the one who delivers mankind from sin.

entries.clue: Port and smack served up by a head of languages (5)

indicatorNotes.served up: in a down clue, 'up' sends TAN upwards, reversing it
indicatorNotes.by: places A and L next to NAT

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to smack them

annotation.surface: A menu of port wine and a slap, oddly served by a language teacher.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink, but it is a harbour town: Natal is a port city in north-east Brazil.
annotation.definitionFit: Natal is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Brazil.

entries.clue: Academic with a say over old artist (9)

blocks.note: a don is a university lecturer
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

annotation.surface: A professor getting the final word on an Old Master.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'having authority over', but it is just a letter: O for an over in cricket, six balls bowled from one end.
annotation.definitionFit: Donatello was a fifteenth-century Florentine sculptor, an artist of the early Renaissance.

entries.clue: Check up about a vacuous gasbag being more annoying (7)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, REIN is read upwards, giving NIER
indicatorNotes.about: NIER goes around A and GG
indicatorNotes.vacuous: empties 'gasbag' of its middle, leaving G…G

blocks.note: rein = check, as in rein in; reversed

annotation.surface: Keeping an eye on a windbag who is growing more irritating.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Check up' looks like a phrase meaning investigate; split it, and 'up' is the instruction to turn REIN around.
annotation.definitionFit: Naggier means more given to nagging, hence more annoying.

entries.clue: Pioneer? Hoskins is one, foremost of liars admitted! (7)

indicatorNotes.admitted: to be admitted is to be let in, so L goes inside SETTER

blocks.note: first letter of liars, placed inside SETTER

annotation.surface: The setter owning up to being first among liars.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter refers to himself by his pseudonym; 'Hoskins is one' means he is a setter.
annotation.definitionFit: A settler is one of the first people to make a home in new territory, a pioneer.

entries.clue: Drug plane smuggling coke? Do this to get out of it! (5)

annotation.definition: Do this to get out of it!

indicatorNotes.smuggling: JET carries C hidden inside it

annotation.surface: A drug-running flight, with the advice to bail out.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the wordplay: 'it' is the plane, and a pilot ejects to get out of a jet.
annotation.definitionFit: Pilots eject from an aircraft to escape it, so ejecting is what you do to get out of the plane.

entries.clue: Move aimlessly around about small English town (5)

indicatorNotes.around: to turn around is to face the other way, so MOPE is read backwards
indicatorNotes.about: 'about' in its sense 'surrounding' puts EPOM on either side of S

blocks.note: to mope is to wander about listlessly; reversed

annotation.surface: Someone drifting listlessly around a little English town.
annotation.walkthrough: Epsom is a Surrey town, home of the Derby horse race.
annotation.definitionFit: Epsom is a market town in Surrey, England.

entries.clue: Editor gets hot hotel food brought up in capital (9)

indicatorNotes.gets: ED is followed by the rest
indicatorNotes.brought up: in a down clue, H GRUB is read upwards

annotation.surface: A newspaper editor served a hot hotel meal in the capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hot' sits beside 'hotel' as if describing the food, but it stands alone as IN, meaning trendy.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Edinburgh is Scotland's seat of government, one capital among many.

entries.clue: Scottish runner first to try marijuana (5)

annotation.surface: A Scottish athlete being the first to try cannabis.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete, but a runner here is a river: the Tweed runs along the Scottish border.
annotation.definitionFit: The Tweed is a river in the Scottish Borders, and rivers are runners in crosswordland.

entries.clue: Dead soon ... heading for tomb for 11 pm? (4-5)

blocks.note: the late X = the dead X

annotation.surface: A gloomy thought about imminent death and a late-hour trip to the grave.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 11 pm as one example of a late-night hour.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: 11 pm is one hour that counts as late in the evening.

entries.clue: French banker fit to be tried in hearing (5)

indicatorNotes.in hearing: says the word should be heard, not read

blocks.note: someone fit to stand trial is legally sane

annotation.surface: A French banker declared mentally fit to stand trial at a court hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'banker' in crosswords is a river, since it has banks; 'in hearing' pretends to be a court hearing.
annotation.definitionFit: The Seine is the river flowing through Paris, a French thing with banks.

entries.clue: Beer imbibed by gut-chucking violent man (5)

indicatorNotes.imbibed by: ALE goes inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.gut-chucking: throws out the middle of 'violent', leaving V…T

blocks.note: ale is beer, placed inside VT

annotation.surface: A thug downing beer and then throwing up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gut-chucking' reads as vomiting, but it means gutting the word: throwing out its insides.
annotation.definitionFit: A man can mean a manservant, and a valet is a gentleman's personal manservant.

entries.clue: I harshly censure a corrupt capital city (9)

blocks.note: to slam is to criticise harshly

annotation.surface: Someone condemning a crooked capital.
annotation.walkthrough: The first word does double duty in the surface as the speaker and in the wordplay as the letter I, used exactly as printed.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Islamabad is Pakistan's seat of government, purpose-built in the 1960s.

entries.clue: One poaching beef in recipe with awful result (7)

indicatorNotes.awful: RESULT is rearranged, made a mess of

blocks.note: R = recipe, the Latin 'take' on prescriptions

annotation.surface: A cook poaching beef to a disastrous result.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poaching beef' sounds like a cooking method, but it means stealing cattle.
annotation.definitionFit: A rustler steals cattle, so is one who poaches beef on the hoof.

entries.clue: Extremely lofty senior officer's a bit off (9)

blocks.note: a super is a police superintendent
high meat or game is going off

annotation.surface: A snooty senior officer whose behaviour is a little out of order.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's reads as 'is', but it is 'has': the officer has the rest after him. A super is British slang for a police superintendent.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the prefix super- intensifies, as 'extremely' does, and high is lofty.

entries.clue: Engineer bore, with bit of sass, gets into bed? (7)

indicatorNotes.with: 'with' means accompanied by, so S is added alongside the rest

annotation.surface: A dull, cheeky engineer slipping between the sheets.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that retiring means going to bed only in one sense.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'retire for the night' means going to bed, and the question mark allows that one sense of retiring.

entries.clue: Conversation doubly offensive about each EU leader (4-1-4)

indicatorNotes.doubly: 'doubly' means twice over, so the offensive appears two times
indicatorNotes.about: 'about' in its sense 'surrounding' puts the two TETs on either side of EA

blocks.note: the Tet Offensive of the Vietnam War, 1968
EA = each, placed between the two TETs

annotation.surface: A doubly insulting chat about every European head of state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' pretends to be an adjective, rude, but it is a noun: the Tet Offensive of 1968.
annotation.definitionFit: A tête-à-tête is a private conversation between two people.

entries.clue: Drunk or sober, male wears satisfactory hats (9)

indicatorNotes.wears: the anagram has M on inside it

annotation.surface: A man, sober or not, wearing hats good enough to pass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk or sober' reads as 'in any state', but 'drunk' scrambles the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Sombreros are wide-brimmed Mexican hats.

entries.clue: Cheats on holiday after 'split' with soprano (4,3)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following, so OFF comes behind the other pieces
indicatorNotes.with: 'with' means accompanied by, so S joins RIP

annotation.surface: A cheating partner off on holiday after breaking up, with a singer in tow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split' in quotes looks like a break-up, but it is a tear.
annotation.definitionFit: To rip someone off is to cheat them.

entries.clue: Old man ignoring final bill? Idiot! (7)

indicatorNotes.ignoring final: drops the last letter of FATHER

blocks.note: old man = father, without its last letter R
a bill is a poster, an ad

annotation.surface: Someone scolding their dad for not paying the last bill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Final bill' seems to go together, but 'final' applies to the old man: FATHER loses its end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from informal insults: someone with a head full of fat rather than brains.

entries.clue: Masculine desire repelled Manchester United player (7)

annotation.surface: A macho footballer's ambitions rebuffed by his football club.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Player' looks like a footballer, but it is an actor: Robert Mitchum.
annotation.definitionFit: Robert Mitchum was a Hollywood actor, and actors are players.

entries.clue: Flash bum around heads of HSBC in High Barnet (7)

indicatorNotes.around: 'around' in its sense 'surrounding' puts MO and CAN on either side of HI
indicatorNotes.heads of: takes the first letters of HSBC and in

blocks.note: in a flash = in a mo, a moment
first letters of HSBC and in
can is US slang for the buttocks

annotation.surface: A flashy show-off hanging about a bank branch in the London suburb of High Barnet.
annotation.walkthrough: High Barnet is a London suburb, but 'barnet' is Cockney rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair), and a Mohican is a tall stripe of hair. HSBC is a British bank.
annotation.definitionFit: A Mohican is a tall ridge of hair down the middle of a shaved head, so a high barnet.

entries.clue: Prison guard's twitch? (9)

blocks.note: bird is slang for a prison term

annotation.surface: A nervous tic on the face of a prison officer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Twitch' looks like a nervous tic, but birders call hunting rare species twitching. 'Bird' is British slang for time in prison.
annotation.definitionFit: Twitching is the British term for chasing rare birds, so to twitch is to birdwatch.

entries.clue: Wife-stealing villain that's heartless as Hoskins? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: an adjective phrase describing the setter's style: bawdy, as Hoskins is

indicatorNotes.heartless: removes the middle letter of BADDY

blocks.note: baddy = villain, without its central D

annotation.surface: A heartless cad running off with someone's wife, likened to the setter.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter owns up again: Hoskins puzzles are famously rude, as 1 across and 22 down in this one show.
annotation.definitionFit: Hoskins's crosswords are known for their smut, so bawdy describes them.

entries.clue: Bum in US court necking a drop of Zinfandel (5)

indicatorNotes.necking: WOO swallows the letters as if drinking them
indicatorNotes.a drop of: takes only the first letter of 'Zinfandel'

blocks.note: to court is to woo; it goes around the rest

annotation.surface: A tramp in an American courtroom swigging red wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a vagrant, but it is the backside; 'US court' looks like a law court, yet 'in US' belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use, flagged by 'in US': American slang for the backside, as in 'up the wazoo'.

entries.clue: Old Mogul emperor seen in bleak barrio (5)

indicatorNotes.seen in: the answer can be seen inside the next words

annotation.surface: An ancient ruler spotted in a grim Latin American neighbourhood.
annotation.walkthrough: A barrio is a Spanish-speaking district; the answer straddles the gap between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Akbar the Great was the third Mughal emperor of India.

entries.clue: A Parisian probing globe going around Mars? (5)

indicatorNotes.probing: to probe is to poke into, so UN pushes inside the globe
indicatorNotes.going around: something going around turns to face the other way, so ORB is read backwards

blocks.note: an orb is a globe, reversed

annotation.surface: A French scientist probing a planet orbiting Mars.
annotation.walkthrough: Mars looks like the planet next to 'globe', but it is a surname: Bruno Mars, the singer.
annotation.definitionFit: Bruno Mars is an American pop singer, so Mars is one person called Bruno.

entries.clue: Speed is ace (5)

blocks.note: a verb here: to rush along
a noun here: a brilliant expert

annotation.surface: Someone declaring that speed is excellent.
annotation.walkthrough: Whizz is also British slang for the drug speed, amphetamine, which makes the surface a drug-user's endorsement.
annotation.definitionFit: Whizz means to rush along, and a whizz is someone brilliant, an ace.

entries.clue: Former inspector reported Treasury department (9)

indicatorNotes.reported: the word is heard, so spelt differently

annotation.surface: An ex-inspector reported to the Treasury.
annotation.walkthrough: The Exchequer is the British government's treasury department, run by the Chancellor.
annotation.definitionFit: The Exchequer is the UK government department in charge of public money.

entries.clue: I'm a boorish lout and I'm very happy about it! (5)

blocks.note: from the brutish human-like creatures in Swift's Gulliver's Travels

annotation.surface: A lout cheerfully proud of his own boorishness.
annotation.walkthrough: The first 'I'm' belongs to the surface: 'I'm a yahoo' works; the second definition is a whole exclamation.
annotation.definitionFit: A yahoo is a coarse lout, and 'yahoo!' is a whoop of joy.

entries.clue: Adore snug pants? That's fraught with peril! (9)

indicatorNotes.pants: British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a mess

annotation.surface: Someone who loves tight trousers, warned it's a risky choice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers (in British usage, underpants), but it is the slang for rubbish that signals the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Dangerous means full of risk, fraught with peril.
